8.  Water Allocation Transfer Request
  In 2017, the City was working on low/moderate housing developments with a housing
  developer. The project was shelved for several reasons and is no longer being pursued.
  The 2017 project did make application for a water allocation for 10.38 acre feet with the
  City identified as the applicant. Now that water allocations from Southern California
  Edison (SCE) are in the near term, the City wants to ensure its current, viable projects
  that are programmed in the current Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) are allocated
  sufficient water to move forward.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize City Staff to submit a request to Southern California Edison to transfer water
  allocations from housing projects no longer being pursued to housing projects at 206 E.
  Whittley and the City Hall Campus.

SUBJECT:  Fiscal Year 2021-2022 Third Quarter Treasurer’s Report

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt the resolution accepting the FY21-22 Third Quarter
Treasurer’s Report.

REPORT SUMMARY: State and Municipal Codes require the Treasurer to submit within
30 days following each fiscal quarter a report summarizing the City’s cash and investment
balances. Attached is the Third Quarter Treasurer’s Report for FY21-22.

The purpose of the report is to inform you on a quarterly basis, the City’s cash and investment
balances, the investment types, yields, and market values, and to ensure you that the City’s
investments are in compliance with the City’s adopted Investment Policy.

The report shows that all of the City’s funds are in compliance with its investment policy. In
general, operating cash is held in US Bank checking accounts and the excess cash is invested
in California’s Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF), less than 04% interest, and various
certificates of deposit (CD5), earning around 1.60% interest, as of March 31, 2022.

The unrestricted cash balance for the third quarter of 2021-2022 totaled $12.01 million. The
unrestricted cash balance for the same quarter in the prior year was $5.52 million, which
included cash for enterprise funds (e.g. Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste) not available for
general government functions. General Fund unrestricted cash was less than $4 million with
negative cash balances in the Harbor Fund. The increase in unrestricted cash can be
attributed to unprecedented growth in visitor-driven revenues over the past twelve months,
significantly exceeding pre-COVID figures, as well as from savings realized by maintaining
many of the cost saving measures implemented in response to the pandemic, While
unrestricted cash balances decreased by $1.16 million from the prior quarter, this is expected
due to the seasonality of visitor-driven tax revenues and the timing of major capital
expenditures.

The cash balance in restricted accounts as of March 31, 2022 totaled $9.53 million, an
increase $104 thousand compared to the quarter ended March 31, 2021. The increase is
primarily attributable to budgeted contributions to the City’s landfill trust account and the timing
of administrative allowance payments from the Successor Agency to unrestricted cash
accounts.

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconference/Virtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed
by the Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result of the
COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health or safety
of attendees,

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. Newly enacted AB 361 provides an exception to these
procedures in order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including
the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EQ N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021. the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required under AS 361

Under AB 361, the City Council can hold virtual meetings without providing notice of the City
Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes the determination that there is a
Governor-proclaimed state of emergency, which the City Council will consider in their
determination, and one of two secondary criteria listed below exists:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; or

   2. The City Council determines that requiring a meeting in person would present an
  imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

COVID-1 9 continues to present an imminent threat to the health or safety of members of the
public, and the Governor’s declaration of a CO VI D-19 emergency still exists. Although vaccines
are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully vaccinated and
remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through person-to-person
contact and those in close proximity. Further, more contagious variants of the disease are now
present in the State and County, the most predominant of which is a new variant of the Omnicron
variant. The County of Los Angeles recently re-instituted some mandates given the rise in cases.
The City’s economy is dependent upon visitors to the island! the presence of which, increases
the likelihood of transmission of the disease. Also, having members of the public attend council
meetings at locations where council members are in attendance due to their desire to avoid
exposure to COVID-19 poses an imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the findings listed above at its April 3, 2022 City Council meeting.
Consistent with the provisions of Government Code Section 54953(e), the findings must be made
every 30 days “after teleconferencing for the first time” under AB 361. Thus, if the City Council
desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each teleconference
location, the City Council must again find that the COVID-19 emergency still exists and that one
of the two following findings can be made: that state or local officials have imposed or
recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, or, that a
result of the COVID-1 9 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health
or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every thirty (30) days, the City
Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming May 17, 2022 meeting and thirty (30)
days thereafter.

It is recommended that the City Council make these findings.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AB 361 at its May 17,
2022 City Council meeting.

SUBJECT:  Resolution Adopting Memorandums of Understanding Between
  the City of Avalon and International Association of Firefighters
  Local 2295, Management, Confidential/Unrepresented Labor
  Associations for the Contract Period July 1, 2022 through June
  30. 2025.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):  Adopt the resolutions adopting Memorandums of
Understanding between the City of Avalon and the International Association of Firefighters
Local 2295, Confidential/Unrepresented and Management labor associations for the
contract period July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.

REPORT SUMMARY: The 2018-2021 Memorandums of Understanding (MOU5) between
the City of Avalon and its five labor associations: International Association of Firefighters
Local 2295 (IAFF), Avalon Harbor Employee Association (AHEA), Avalon Municipal
Employee Association (AMEA), Management and Confidential Employees were adopted
on July 16, 2019.

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the financial impact of statewide shutdowns,
emergency modifications were made to the MOUs on August 4, 2020. These modifications
included:
  1. All uniform allowances eliminated. Uniforms would only be purchased on an as
  needed basis.
  2. Travel reimbursements, also known as commuter book reimbursements (2
  annually), eliminated. (Partially reinstated on December 31, 2021.)
  3. Education reimbursements eliminated.
  4. Floating Holidays (2 days/16 hours of paid time off) eliminated.
  5. When calculating overtime, hours worked” would only be defined as hours actually
  worked. Vacation hours would no longer be factored into overtime calculations.
  6. Accumulation of comp time was eliminated.
  7. All longevity increases frozen. No retroactive pay would be accumulated.
  8. Employees could no longer cash out administrative paid time off. A maximum 30 to
  40 hours would be carried over year to year.
  9. Volunteer Drill Pay, Special Drill Pay were restricted and available only at the Fire
  Chiefs discretion.
  10.Training and Leave Pay, and Association Representative Leave is eliminated.
  11. Cost of Living and Classification/Compensation Studies were postponed.
Effective March 17, 2020 all step increases were frozen for all employees and a
notification was made indicating no retroactive pay would be accumulated during this time
period.
 These modifications resulted in significant cost savings and helped the City to remain
solvent during a very tumultuous time.

Though there is still some uncertainty with regard to revenue projections and COVID-19,
as the budgetary crisis has passed, the new MOUs restore all of the emergency
modifications to the MOUs implemented on August 4, 2020.

To counter the wage freeze that has been in place since 2020, the new MOUs provide all
employees covered by the MOUs a wage increase annually for the terms of the
agreements.

Additionally, the new MOUs sunset the Retiree Medical provision that previously granted
healthcare benefits equivalent to the City paid maximum contribution to all retiring
employees with 20 or more years of service with the City. Current employees will maintain
this benefit; however, it will no longer be available to future employees. This amendment
will limit the financial liability of the City.

The City Manager has worked cooperatively with all five labor associations and has met
with each union multiple times since February 18, 2022; however1 at this time, agreements
have only been reached with the IAFF, Management and Confidential/Unrepresented labor
associations.

FISCAL IMPACTS: Fiscal implications of these MOUs have been integrated into the
Fiscal Year 2022-2023 Budget.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Fiscal and organizational stability.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION:  The current
MOUs will expire on June 30, 2022.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

Permit from Island Bikes to Martin Leyva, permitting 30 electric bicycles for rental and guided
tours. 2. If a transfer is approved, require Leyva to return to City Council with an operations
plan adhering to all conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal Code and Resolution 21-07 by
no later than April 30, 2024.

REPORT SUMMARY: On March 14, 2022, Martin Leyva submitted a Transportation Permit
Application to transfer 30 electric bicycle permits from Island Bikes, previously owned by
Matthew Affolder.

On March 28, 2022, City Staff requested Levya provide supplemental information to his
application including:

  -  Location on where bikes will be served.
  -  Description of plan to work with traffic flows.

no brick-and-mortar location had been submitted for approval.

On March 16. 2021, the City Council approved the transfer of 30 electric bicycle permits from
Catalina Tours to Island Bikes. Though the transfer was approved, the City Council required
that the new permit holder’s operations plan be approved before conducting business. On April
6, 2021, the City Council considered an operations plan with a brick and mortar rental facility
located at 220 Metropole Avenue. On July 6, 2021 the City Council considered an operations
plan with a brick and mortar rental facility located at 131 Metropole, Unit #161 E. Both
operations plans were denied as the locations present safety and traffic flow concerns.
 Per the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Chapter 5, Section 14.02: transportation permits are
valid for a period of three years and may be renewed for a subsequent three-year period if the
operator is in compliance with the terms of their permit and the AMC.

electric bicycles for rental and guided tours. If approved Island Bikes must adhere to all
conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal Code. If changes in their compliance with the
conditions occur, they are required to notify the City for approval.

REPORT SUMMARY: During the April 6, 2021 City Council Meeting, the City Council
authorized the transfer of 30 electric bike permits from Tour Catalina to Island Bikes. The
transfer was approved contingent on the new operator, Matthew Affolder, providing an
operation plan to the City Council for their review and approval.

Among the requirements set forth by the City Council, the operator was required to find an
alternative location than originally proposed to conduct business. The original location at 220
Metropole was not authorized due to safety concerns.

Island Bikes provided a new operation plan to City Staff on June 21, 2021. The new operation
plan proposes 131 Metropole Unit #161 E as the business’s brick-and-mortar location to
conduct rentals. This location was proposed to the City Council as a brick-and-mortar
operations center by Catalina Electric Bikes on April 6, 2021. A motion was made by Mayor
Anni Marshall to grant Catalina Electric Bikes 15 electric bike permits on the contingency that a
different location be determined; however, the motion did not carry and Catalina Electric Bikes
was not authorized a transportation permit for operations as the facts presented did not
demonstrate a need for the permits.

There is no current lease for the property; however, Island Bikes provided an email from the
Hermosa Hotel Manager indicating his interest in renting the property for the purpose of
electric bike rentals.

Staff is always concerned with the safety aspect, stagingltraining area, congestion, and the
absence of restricted routes for electric bicycles.

The Metropole Avenue is a major thoroughfare with limited pedestrian activity. However, the
area around 131 Metropole Avenue is more prone to pedestrian traffic with residents and
 visitors using the public easement to access the Catalina Island Museum as well as the public
staircase to Calle Del Sol. The area immediately beyond the public easement is a one hour
parking zone.

If the one hour parking zone is occupied by a vehicle the operator indicated that they may, in
essence, double park the bikes so they may depart and return to the brick-and-mortar location.
If the location is approved by the City Council, Island Bikes indicated they would be interested
in requesting a commercial loading/unloading zone be established at the location to better
facilitate their operations. Staff would not be in support of this request as my set precedence in
the future.

The other terms of the transportation permit indicate Island Bikes will maintain the same routes
(operation on all City of Avalon streets and pending approval of Catalina Island Company
roads), hours of operation (8 am. to dusk), mandatory helmet use and use of up to 30 bikes.
The applicant will stay current with all licenses, fees, pay admission tax of 4% and provide a
clearly marked patrol bike to ensure their patrons are following the rules.

If approved Island Bikes must adhere to all conditions set forth in the Avalon Municipal Code,
the City’s Electric Bike Rental Policy, and other conditions the City Council imposes to provide
for safe operation of the business. If changes in their ability to comply with the conditions
occur, they are required to notify the City for approval.

SUBJECT:  Water Allocation Transfer Request

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Authorize City Staff to submit a request to Southern
California Edison to transfer water allocations from housing projects no longer being
pursued to housing projects at 206 E. Whittley and the City Hall campus.

REPORT SUMMARY:  In 2017, the City was working on low/moderate housing
developments with housing developer Cottle & Cottle. That project was shelved for
several reasons and is no longer being pursued.

The 2017 project did make application for a water allocation for 10.38 acre feet with the
City identified as the applicant. Now that water allocations from Southern California
Edison (SCE) are in the near term, the City wants to ensure its current, viable projects
that are programmed in the current Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) are allocated
sufficient water to move forward.

The first project proposes additional units at 206 E. Whittley Avenue a low/mod site.
  —

The City is currently rehabilitating the sewer that services the property for the existing 4-
units. This will be followed by the major rehabilitation of the existing units and demolition
of the one bedroom cottage on the eastern side of the property. This is programmed under
Capital Project #205015. An additional building is proposed to build an additional five
units plus a replacement unit for the cottage for a total of 6-units in the new structure. The
existing 4-unit structure plus the additional 6-unit building could yield 10 potential units on
the site for low/moderate housing operated by the City. This is programmed under Capital
Project #205016.

The second project is the potential Workforce Housing Project proposed to be constructed
on the City Hall Campus. The housing will be located on a pad to be constructed within
the scope of work associated with the Five Corners Project. The pad will be created along
Tremont Street and along the southern side of City Hall. This housing is proposed in
concept to serve the workforce housing needs for City operations as well as short-term
housing for City contractors. Concept plans to date propose a project in the range of 17
units. This is programmed under Capital Project #205014.
